title: Studying In-service Teacher Professional Development on Purposeful Integration of Engineering into K-12 STEM Teaching (Research to Practice)
venue: American Society for Engineering Education Conference Proceedings
extended_summary:
This paper examines how two graduate-level professional development courses supported in-service K-12 teachers’ integration of engineering into STEM teaching. The authors focus on a recurring problem in STEM education: although teachers see value in engineering, many feel underprepared or anxious about implementing engineering practices and design-based instruction in their own classrooms. The study is framed around teacher self-efficacy and social justice-oriented STEM teaching.

The intervention consisted of two courses, Enhancing Mathematics with STEM and Engineering in the K-12 Classroom, embedded in a grant-funded STEM teacher leadership program. The courses included readings, short lectures, guest speakers from engineering and STEM fields, hands-on engineering activities, vertically aligned collaboration across grade bands, lesson planning, microteaching, peer feedback, and reflection. Teachers also worked on 5E lesson plans and engineering unit plans, with the engineering course emphasizing engineering design activities connected to community needs, societal impacts, and equity.

The participants were 18 in-service teachers from elementary, middle, and high school science, math, and computer science contexts in urban or suburban high-need districts in the United States. Data came from autobiographies, reflections, focus groups, lesson plans, microteaching, questionnaires, and instructor field notes. The authors conclude that the courses increased teachers’ self-efficacy for teaching engineering, that active learning and structured collaboration were important supports, and that explicitly linking engineering to social justice and societal problems helped teachers see engineering as relevant and meaningful. The paper also suggests that hands-on practice, feedback, and reflection were key mechanisms for teacher growth.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study of a professional development program with thematic analysis of reflections, focus groups, lesson plans, and observations. It provides credible descriptive evidence, but it is not experimental and reports no causal effect sizes.
impact_tier_rationale: The program appears to have had meaningful benefits for a small group of in-service teachers, especially on self-efficacy and planning capacity, but the paper does not report quantitative impacts on student learning or system-level outcomes. The observed impact is promising but modest and localized.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 in-service K-12 teachers, the study found increased self-efficacy and confidence for teaching STEM and engineering after two graduate STEM pedagogy courses. Early on, most participants reported low confidence with engineering integration, but by the end of the second course all participants reported strong self-efficacy; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, focus groups, microteaching lesson plans, instructor observations/field notes, and autobiography/reflection assignments focused on STEM/engineering teaching self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The courses appeared to improve teachers’ pedagogical planning, collaboration, and ability to design integrated STEM lessons using engineering design and 5E microteaching. Teachers reported that vertical PLC-style collaboration, hands-on activities, peer feedback, and reflection helped them develop practical skills for lesson design and implementation; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Integrated STEM lesson plans, engineering unit plans, microteaching performance, peer feedback, and participant reflections/focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the professional development increased teachers’ confidence to advocate for STEM/engineering integration with colleagues and administrators and to frame engineering as a social-justice-oriented school practice. Findings are qualitative and program-level, showing likely influence on teacher agency and potential school implementation rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Participant reflections and focus groups describing advocacy, STEM teacher identity, and perceptions of school-based implementation
